_meta.source: MoHFW eSanjeevani Teleconsultation Protocol, WHO Primary Care Guidelines, AIIMS Triage Manual
_meta.description: Official triage protocol rules used for RAG cross-validation

EMERGENCY.description: Life-threatening. Patient needs emergency services NOW.

URGENT.description: Potentially serious. Risk of deterioration if untreated.

ROUTINE.description: Non-urgent. Can wait for scheduled appointment.

protocols.title: Acute Chest Pain Protocol
protocols.criteria: Any patient describing chest pain, especially with: radiation to arm/jaw, sweating, breathlessness, or nausea.
protocols.action: Immediately escalate. Advise patient not to exert. Alert emergency services if available.
key_questions: Is the pain constant or does it come and go?
Does the pain go to your arm or jaw?
Are you sweating more than usual?
Are you finding it hard to breathe?
Do you have a known heart condition?
protocols.contraindications: Do NOT reassure and dismiss. Every chest pain in adults >35 is cardiac until proven otherwise.

protocols.title: Stroke Recognition Protocol (FAST)
protocols.criteria: Sudden onset of: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, at any Time.
protocols.action: Call emergency services immediately. Time to treatment is critical — every minute of stroke = 1.9 million neurons lost.
key_questions: Did this happen suddenly?
Is one side of their face drooping?
Can they lift both arms equally?
Is their speech unclear or strange?
protocols.contraindications: Never wait to see if symptoms resolve. TIA can precede full stroke.

protocols.title: Respiratory Distress Protocol
protocols.criteria: Patient unable to complete sentences due to breathlessness, bluish lips, or SpO2 < 90%.
protocols.action: Emergency escalation. Sitting upright, open airway. Alert emergency services.
key_questions: Can you speak a full sentence without stopping to breathe?
Are your lips or fingertips turning blue?
Do you have an oximeter reading?
protocols.contraindications: Do not put patient on hold. Keep call open.

protocols.title: High Fever with Warning Signs Protocol
protocols.criteria: Fever > 38.5°C (101.3°F) with: altered consciousness, stiff neck, rash, or not responding to antipyretics.
protocols.action: Urgent consultation. If confusion present, escalate to Emergency.
key_questions: How high is the fever?
Is the patient confused or difficult to wake?
Is there any rash?
Is the neck stiff?
Has fever lasted more than 3 days?
protocols.contraindications: High fever in infants <3 months = EMERGENCY regardless of other signs.

protocols.title: Obstetric Emergency Protocol
protocols.criteria: Pregnant patient with: heavy vaginal bleeding, severe abdominal pain, seizures, or absent fetal movement.
protocols.action: Emergency escalation. Advise patient to lie on left side. Alert emergency services.
key_questions: How many months pregnant are you?
Is there heavy bleeding?
Is the pain constant or in waves?
Can you feel the baby moving?
Do you have high blood pressure?
protocols.contraindications: Never reassure pregnant patient with bleeding — always escalate.

protocols.title: Pediatric Emergency Protocol
protocols.criteria: Child under 5 with: high fever (>39°C), seizure, difficulty breathing, not feeding, or altered consciousness.
protocols.action: Emergency escalation for infants. Urgent for older children.
key_questions: How old is the child?
What is the temperature?
Is the child responsive?
Is the child eating/drinking?
Has the child had a fit?
protocols.contraindications: All fevers in newborns (<28 days) are EMERGENCY.

protocols.title: Mental Health Crisis Protocol
protocols.criteria: Patient expresses: suicidal thoughts, plan to harm self or others, or has already attempted self-harm.
protocols.action: Emergency escalation. Do NOT leave patient alone. Contact emergency services.
key_questions: Are you having thoughts of hurting yourself?
Do you have a plan?
Have you tried to hurt yourself before?
Is anyone with you right now?
protocols.contraindications: Never dismiss suicidal ideation. Always take seriously.

protocols.title: Diabetic Emergency Protocol
protocols.criteria: Known diabetic with: altered consciousness, blood sugar <50 mg/dL, or inability to take oral intake.
protocols.action: If conscious: give sugar immediately. If unconscious: emergency services.
key_questions: Is the patient a known diabetic?
What is the blood sugar reading?
Is the patient conscious and able to swallow?
Has the patient taken insulin recently?
protocols.contraindications: Never give anything by mouth to an unconscious patient.

protocols.title: Suspected Infectious Disease Protocol
protocols.criteria: Patient with: fever + rash, or fever + bleeding, or fever + severe myalgia (dengue suspicion), or cough >2 weeks + night sweats (TB suspicion).
protocols.action: Urgent consultation. If hemorrhagic signs present, escalate to Emergency.
key_questions: How long has the fever lasted?
Any bleeding from nose, gums, or in urine/stool?
Any rash on body?
Any recent travel to endemic areas?
protocols.contraindications: Dengue with bleeding = Emergency, not Urgent.

protocols.title: Acute Abdominal Emergency Protocol
protocols.criteria: Severe abdominal pain with: rigidity, vomiting blood, or blood in stool with hypotension signs.
protocols.action: Emergency escalation. Keep patient nil by mouth. Emergency services.
key_questions: Is the pain constant or wave-like?
Is the stomach hard and rigid?
Any vomiting or blood in stool?
Any recent surgery or injury to abdomen?
protocols.contraindications: Do not give painkillers without doctor consultation — may mask signs.
